awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: CNS Core: Small: Model, Design, and Implement Entanglement Routing Protocols for Quantum Networks
awd_abstract_narration:
The recently released "A Strategic Vision for America’s Quantum Networks" driven by the National Quantum Initiative Act addressed the importance of quantum networks on future communication security and computing advancement.  Quantum networks supplement traditional networks, e.g., the Internet, and enable important applications such as secure key distribution, clock synchronization, secure remote computation, and distributed consensus, most of which cannot be easily and efficiently achieved by the classical Internet. This project focuses on a fundamental network service for quantum networks, namely quantum entanglement routing. If successful, the research outcomes of this project will be transformative as they will provide critical networking services and tasks such as secure communication and time synchronization, which in turn, will enable emerging and future services including IoT, edge computing, and their applications. 

To address quantum entanglement routing, this project will develop quantum network models that are consistent with results from experimental physics, while applying computer network design techniques and research methodologies to quantum networks. The proposed models will account for practical considerations from network protocol design, such as arbitrary network topologies, multiple concurrent sources and destinations that compete for resources, fidelity and purification, limited capacity at each node, as well as the fact that nodes only know localized short-lived link-state information. As such, the expected contributions of the proposed research are as follows: 1) Exploration of different routing metrics; 2) Development of offline and online contention-free routing protocols; 3) Design of efficient topologies for quantum networking; 4) Evaluation of the proposed algorithms using analytical models as well as a custom simulator; and 5) Implementation of the proposed protocols with real quantum devices.  The network models, algorithms, protocols, and experimental tools developed in this project will be made available to the networking research community to help jump-start research efforts on quantum networks, e.g., exploring ink layer and transport layer services.  The project will leverage the visibility and timeliness of quantum computing and quantum networking to recruit first-generation students as well as students from under-represented populations.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Future quantum technologies are expected to transform secure communication, computing, and sensing. One of the key building blocks of these technologies is the quantum network, which connects quantum devices using a uniquely quantum resource called entanglement. Entanglement links particles such as photons or atoms so that their properties remain correlated even when separated by long distances. Efficiently creating, distributing, and managing entanglement across a network is a major scientific and engineering challenge that must be solved before a large-scale “quantum internet” becomes possible.

A central goal of this project was to adapt ideas from classical computer networking—such as routing algorithms, network topologies, and resource management—to the fundamentally different environment of quantum communication. Unlike classical data packets, quantum information cannot be copied and is highly sensitive to noise and loss. To address these challenges, the project developed models and protocols that account for practical constraints in quantum networks, including limited quantum memory, imperfect entanglement fidelity, and competition among multiple users attempting to access shared quantum resources. These advances contribute to the intellectual foundation needed for scalable quantum communication networks.

This NSF collaborative research project brought together expertise in physics, electrical engineering, and computer science to study how quantum networks can be designed and implemented. The collaboration involved research teams at Purdue University and the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC). While the UCSC team focused primarily on network protocol design and software tools, the Purdue research group concentrated on the physical implementation and fundamental physics of atom–photon quantum networking, developing both theoretical models and experimental platforms.

One major outcome of the collaboration was the development of a quantum network simulator for atom–atom entanglement generation. This work, conducted jointly with collaborators at UCSC, produced software modules capable of modeling the physical processes involved in establishing entanglement between distant atomic nodes. The simulator incorporates realistic experimental parameters, including photon loss, multi-photon noise, and quantum memory operations. By bridging physical quantum hardware with network-level simulation, this tool provides researchers with a platform to test new routing protocols and distributed algorithms before deploying them in real quantum systems.

On the physics side, the project advanced the development of atom–photon quantum network platforms, which use cold atomic ensembles as remote quantum nodes connected by flying photons. Particularly, we discovered the symmetry-protected two-photon coherence, demonstrating that entangled photon pairs under some certain time-space symmetry can maintain their coherence even in the presence of optical loss and noise. Another study experimentally revealed the bosonic exchange symmetry of photon pairs in the time domain, providing new insight into the fundamental quantum behavior of light. These technologies form the physical foundation for future quantum networks capable of distributing entanglement across multiple devices.

The project also contributed to a new architecture for distributed quantum computing based on the concept of a Shared Quantum Gate Processing Unit (S-QGPU), in which multiple small quantum processors are connected through a shared resource that performs remote quantum gate operations. This architecture, developed in work including Distributed quantum computing with photons and atomic memories (Adv. Quantum Technol., 2023) and subsequent studies, demonstrates how atom–photon hybrid systems could enable scalable distributed quantum computing across networked devices.

The project further led to a U.S. patent application, “Quantum computing apparatus with photons and atomic memories,” reflecting the potential technological and commercial impact of this hybrid photon–atom approach to distributed quantum computing.

In addition to advancing scientific knowledge, the project provided training opportunities for graduate and undergraduate students in the rapidly growing field of quantum information science and engineering. Students gained interdisciplinary experience working across physics, networking, and experimental hardware development. Through regular collaboration meetings between Purdue and UCSC, students from different disciplines learned to communicate across fields and contribute to the development of emerging quantum technologies. These activities contribute to workforce development in quantum information science and help prepare the next generation of scientists and engineers.

Overall, this project helped bridge the gap between quantum networking theory and physical implementation, advancing both the scientific understanding and technological foundations needed for future quantum communication networks and distributed quantum computing systems.
